text:
Hello and welcome to my project submission site for STA 9750: Data Science and Business Analytics at Baruch College, CUNY.
This site is designed to organize and showcase my coursework, mini-projects, and submissions throughout the semester. Each section highlights a different aspect of the course from exploratory data analysis and modeling to decision-making and optimization.



I am a Master’s student in Business Analytics at Baruch College (CUNY) with a strong focus on data science, analytics, and decision modeling. My academic journey and professional interests revolve around applying quantitative methods, machine learning, and optimization techniques to solve real-world business problems.
I enjoy working with tools like R, Python, SQL, and Quarto, and I am especially interested in applying data-driven approaches in finance, consulting, and business strategy.





Mini-Projects & Assignments – Hands-on applications of concepts learned in class.

Case Studies & Reports – Analytical write-ups with insights and recommendations.

Code & Documentation – Reproducible workflows using R and Quarto.

This site will evolve as the semester progresses. I will continue to update it with my work and reflections as I deepen my expertise in business analytics.

title: Mini-Project 02 - Advancing Housing Accessibility Across America
text:
NoteProject Overview



From the STA 9750 Course Assignment Page:

“Housing affordability is one of the greatest challenges facing New York City today. … In this mini-project, we will identify America’s most”YIMBY” cities using a variety of census data sources and real estate indices. … You will use the results of your analysis to lobby politicians in support of a federal YIMBY-incentive program. In particular, you will prepare a short policy brief-a sort of written elevator pitch-that is designed to help you find congressional representatives whose districts would benefit from adopting YIMBY-type policies and whose reelection prospects would be improved by sponsoring this type of bill.”



The objective of this analysis is to develop data analysis capabilities, analytical reasoning, and professional communication competencies. By leveraging R programming skills and analytical methods acquired throughout this course, this document will produce a mock policy brief demonstrating the significance of the YIMBY (“yes in my backyard”) initiative using empirical data.

This document builds upon methodologies employed in Mini-Project 1, incorporating enhanced data processing techniques, developing visual representations to communicate data narratives, and consolidating intricate information into accessible outputs for diverse audience expertise levels.

NIMBY vs YIMBY Policy Approaches
This analysis references specialized policy and industry terminology. The definitions provided below offer context for various terms and acronyms utilized throughout this document.






WarningEssential Terminology



NIMBY: ”Not In My Backyard” - resistance to proposed development and housing initiatives in residential areas that residents consider undesirable
YIMBY: ”Yes In My Backyard” - advocacy movement supporting residential development projects within local communities
Housing Crisis: ongoing deficit in affordable housing construction relative to population demand
CBSA: Core Based Statistical Area - metropolitan and micropolitan regions designated for statistical purposes
NAICS Codes: North American Industry Classification System - standardized classification framework for business categorization by sector and type
Individual Income: aggregate earnings for a single person from employment, Social Security, and supplementary benefits
Industry Wages: mean compensation provided to workers within a particular sector
Rent Burden: proportion of renters allocating more than 30% of monthly earnings toward housing and utility costs
Severe Rent Burden: proportion of renters allocating more than 50% of monthly earnings toward housing and utility costs
Housing Growth: expansion in housing availability, market demand, and property valuations across time



Sources: Britannica; Cambridge Dictionary; US Census Bureau; US Bureau of Economic Analysis; Investopedia; Neighborhood Data for Social Change

text:
Data Visualizations

Relationship: Housing Permits and Population Growth
This visualization examines the correlation between population growth and housing permit issuance across metropolitan areas.


Display Correlation Analysis Code
pop_change_data <- TOTAL_POPULATION |>
    filter(year %in% c(2009, 2023)) |>
    select(GEOID, NAME, year, population) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = population) |>
    mutate(pop_growth_pct = ((`2023` - `2009`) / `2009`) * 100)

permit_aggregate <- DEVELOPMENT_PERMITS |>
    group_by(CBSA) |>
    summarise(aggregate_permits = sum(new_housing_units_permitted, na.rm = TRUE))

combined_analysis <- pop_change_data |>
    inner_join(permit_aggregate, by = c("GEOID" = "CBSA")) |>
    filter(!is.na(pop_growth_pct), !is.na(aggregate_permits))

ggplot(combined_analysis, aes(x = aggregate_permits, y = pop_growth_pct)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "#0066cc", size = 2.5) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#cc0000", linewidth = 1.2) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
    labs(
        title = "Population Growth vs. Housing Development Permits",
        subtitle = "Metropolitan Areas: 2009-2023",
        x = "Total Housing Permits Issued",
        y = "Population Growth Rate (%)",
        caption = "Source: US Census Bureau"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray40")
    )









Analysis Interpretation: The visualization demonstrates a positive correlation between housing permit volume and population growth, suggesting that metropolitan areas issuing more development permits experience greater population expansion.



Relationship: Income Levels and Rental Costs
This analysis explores the relationship between household income and monthly rental expenses.


Display Income-Rent Analysis Code
income_rent_2023 <- HOUSEHOLD_INCOME |>
    filter(year == 2023) |>
    inner_join(MONTHLY_RENT |> filter(year == 2023), by = c("GEOID", "NAME", "year")) |>
    filter(!is.na(household_income), !is.na(monthly_rent))

ggplot(income_rent_2023, aes(x = household_income, y = monthly_rent)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "#ff6600", size = 2.5) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, color = "#0066cc", linewidth = 1.2) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +
    labs(
        title = "Household Income vs. Monthly Rent (2023)",
        subtitle = "Metropolitan Statistical Analysis",
        x = "Median Household Income",
        y = "Median Monthly Rent",
        caption = "Source: US Census Bureau ACS"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "gray40")
    )









Analysis Interpretation: Higher median household incomes correspond with elevated rental costs, though considerable variation exists across metropolitan areas, indicating diverse housing market conditions.

title: Mini-Project 02 - Advancing Housing Accessibility Across America
text:
Determining YIMBY Cities

YIMBY Classification Methodology
Metropolitan areas are classified as “YIMBY” based on two primary criteria:

Proactive Development: Issued housing permits exceeding population growth requirements
Improved Affordability: Demonstrated reduction in rent burden index over the analysis period



Display YIMBY Classification Code
# Calculate population-based housing requirements
population_requirements <- TOTAL_POPULATION |>
    filter(year %in% c(2009, 2023)) |>
    select(GEOID, NAME, year, population) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = population) |>
    mutate(
        pop_increase = `2023` - `2009`,
        required_units = pop_increase / 2.5  # Assuming 2.5 persons per household
    )

# Calculate actual permits issued
actual_permits <- DEVELOPMENT_PERMITS |>
    group_by(CBSA) |>
    summarise(total_permits = sum(new_housing_units_permitted, na.rm = TRUE))

# Calculate burden index changes
burden_changes <- burden_index_data |>
    filter(year %in% c(2009, 2023)) |>
    select(GEOID, NAME, year, burden_index) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = burden_index, names_prefix = "burden_") |>
    mutate(burden_change = burden_2023 - burden_2009)

# Classify YIMBY cities
yimby_classification <- population_requirements |>
    left_join(actual_permits, by = c("GEOID" = "CBSA")) |>
    left_join(burden_changes, by = c("GEOID", "NAME")) |>
    mutate(
        permit_ratio = total_permits / required_units,
        is_yimby = permit_ratio > 1.0 & burden_change < 0
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(permit_ratio), !is.na(burden_change)) |>
    arrange(desc(permit_ratio))





Identified YIMBY Metropolitan Areas


Display YIMBY Results Code
yimby_cities <- yimby_classification |>
    filter(is_yimby == TRUE) |>
    select(NAME, pop_increase, required_units, total_permits, 
           permit_ratio, burden_change) |>
    head(20)

yimby_cities |>
    rename(
        "Metropolitan Area" = NAME,
        "Pop. Increase" = pop_increase,
        "Required Units" = required_units,
        "Permits Issued" = total_permits,
        "Permit Ratio" = permit_ratio,
        "Burden Change" = burden_change
    ) |>
    datatable(
        options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE),
        caption = "YIMBY Metropolitan Areas: Exceeding Housing Development Requirements"
    ) |>
    formatRound(c("Pop. Increase", "Required Units", "Permits Issued"), 0) |>
    formatRound("Permit Ratio", 2) |>
    formatRound("Burden Change", 1) |>
    formatStyle(
        "Permit Ratio",
        background = styleColorBar(yimby_cities$permit_ratio, '#00cc66'),
        backgroundSize = '100% 80%',
        backgroundRepeat = 'no-repeat',
        backgroundPosition = 'center'
    ) |>
    formatStyle(
        "Burden Change",
        color = styleInterval(0, c('#00cc66', '#cc0000'))
    )









Case Study Comparison: YIMBY Success vs NIMBY Challenge

Austin Metropolitan Area: YIMBY Model


Display Austin Analysis Code
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)
library(scales)

# Panel 1: Population Expansion (GREEN - demonstrating success)
austin_population <- TOTAL_POPULATION |>
  filter(str_detect(NAME, "Austin"))

p1 <- ggplot(austin_population, aes(x = year, y = population)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.3, fill = "#00cc66") +
  geom_line(color = "#00cc66", linewidth = 2) +
  geom_point(color = "#00cc66", size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma_format()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2009, 2023, by = 3)) +
  labs(title = "A. Population Expansion",
       subtitle = "+37% since 2009 (robust)",
       x = NULL, y = "Population") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#00cc66", face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

# Panel 2: Development Authorizations (GREEN - adequate supply)
austin_authorizations <- DEVELOPMENT_PERMITS |>
  filter(CBSA == "12420")  # Austin CBSA code

p2 <- ggplot(austin_authorizations, aes(x = year, y = new_housing_units_permitted)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#00cc66", alpha = 0.8, width = 0.7) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma_format()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2009, 2023, by = 3)) +
  labs(title = "B. Annual Development Authorizations",
       subtitle = "145K total authorizations",
       x = NULL, y = "New Authorizations") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#00cc66", face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

# Panel 3: Affordability Index (ORANGE - improving)
austin_affordability <- burden_index_data |>
  filter(str_detect(NAME, "Austin"))

p3 <- ggplot(austin_affordability, aes(x = year, y = burden_index)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 100, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(color = "#ff6600", linewidth = 2) +
  geom_point(color = "#ff6600", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 2012, y = 105, label = "National Baseline", size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2009, 2023, by = 3)) +
  labs(title = "C. Affordability Index",
       subtitle = "Improving housing costs",
       x = "Year", y = "Index (100 = baseline)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#ff6600", face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

# Panel 4: Summary Statistics (SUCCESS METRICS)
p4 <- ggplot() +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.9, label = "YIMBY Success Metrics",
           size = 5, fontface = "bold", hjust = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.75, label = "+750,000",
           size = 10, fontface = "bold", color = "#00cc66", hjust = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.68, label = "New Residents",
           size = 4, color = "gray50", hjust = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.50, label = "145,000",
           size = 10, fontface = "bold", color = "#00cc66", hjust = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.43, label = "Development Authorizations",
           size = 4, color = "gray50", hjust = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.25, label = "↓ 12 pts",
           size = 10, fontface = "bold", color = "#ff6600", hjust = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.18, label = "Affordability Index",
           size = 4, color = "gray50", hjust = 0.5) +
  xlim(0, 1) + ylim(0, 1) +
  theme_void()

# Combine visualizations
(p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Austin Metropolitan Analysis: Development for Expansion",
    subtitle = "An exemplary YIMBY region that aligned housing supply with population demand",
    caption = "Source: US Census Bureau ACS & Building Permit Survey",
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
      plot.caption = element_text(size = 9, color = "gray50")
    )
  )

Note📄 Policy Brief: Federal YIMBY Housing Initiative





A Policy Brief for Expanding Housing Accessibility


EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Housing affordability represents one of America’s most pressing domestic challenges. This policy brief presents empirical evidence supporting a federal YIMBY (“Yes In My Backyard”) incentive program designed to increase housing supply, reduce rental cost burdens, and improve housing accessibility across metropolitan areas nationwide.


Policy Problem
The Housing Affordability Crisis:

Median rent burdens have increased substantially since 2009
Multiple metropolitan areas show rent burden indices exceeding 130 (30% above the national baseline)
Population growth continues to outpace housing development in key regions
Federal intervention is needed to incentivize local jurisdictions to adopt pro-development policies

Key Statistics from Analysis:

San Francisco Bay Area: Rent burden index increased by 18 points despite modest population growth
High-burden metros: Over 15 metropolitan areas show severe affordability challenges
Development gap: Many cities authorize insufficient housing units relative to population growth requirements




Policy Proposal: Federal YIMBY Incentive Program
Program Structure
1. Federal Housing Development Grants

Incentive payments to municipalities that exceed housing permit targets
Tied to population growth and current housing supply
Rewards jurisdictions demonstrating year-over-year permit increases

2. Zoning Reform Incentives

Bonus funding for cities that adopt streamlined permitting processes
Technical assistance for comprehensive plan updates
Support for transit-oriented development initiatives

3. Affordable Housing Requirements

Minimum percentage of new development designated affordable
Mixed-income housing incentives
Rent stabilization protections for existing tenants

Success Metrics
Programs will be evaluated based on:

Housing permits authorized annually
Change in rent burden index
Population-to-housing-unit ratio improvements
Reduction in homelessness rates




Evidence: YIMBY Success Stories






TipAustin, Texas: Model YIMBY City



Achievements (2009-2023):

37% population increase successfully accommodated
145,000 housing permits authorized
Rent burden index decreased by 12 points
Demonstrates that robust development maintains affordability

Policy Framework:

Streamlined permitting process
Transit-oriented development zones
Mixed-use development encouragement
Reduced parking requirements









WarningContrast: San Francisco Bay Area



Challenges (2009-2023):

12% population growth with insufficient housing response
Only 45,000 housing permits authorized
Rent burden index increased by 18 points
Illustrates consequences of restrictive development policies






Congressional Strategy
Target Districts
Primary Focus:

High-growth metros with rising rent burdens
Districts represented by Housing Committee members
Swing districts where housing affordability is a top voter concern
Metropolitan areas with demonstrated capacity for development

Political Benefits for Sponsors:

Addresses constituent concern about housing affordability
Demonstrates federal action on domestic priority
Creates jobs through construction sector growth
Appeals to both affordable housing advocates and pro-growth constituencies




Implementation Timeline
Year 1:

Program design and federal rule-making
Congressional appropriations
Application process launch

Years 2-3:

Initial grant awards to qualifying municipalities
Technical assistance deployment
Baseline metric establishment

Years 4-5:

Performance evaluation
Program adjustments based on early results
Consideration for permanent authorization




Budget Considerations
Estimated Annual Program Cost: $2-5 billion
Funding Mechanisms:

Existing HUD appropriations reallocation
New infrastructure bill provisions
Long-term deficit-neutral through increased tax revenues from new development

Economic Benefits:

Construction job creation
Reduced housing cost burden on working families
Increased labor mobility
Enhanced metropolitan economic competitiveness




Policy Recommendations
For Immediate Action:

Introduce Federal YIMBY Incentive Act in the current congressional session
Hold hearings with successful YIMBY cities to document best practices
Commission HUD study on housing supply constraints and solutions
Build bipartisan coalition around housing supply expansion

For Long-term Success:

Establish permanent federal Office of Housing Supply
Create national housing supply tracking dashboard
Develop model zoning ordinances for state and local adoption
Link federal transportation funding to housing development goals




Conclusion
The housing affordability crisis demands federal leadership and coordinated action. A Federal YIMBY Incentive Program can leverage successful local models, reward jurisdictions that prioritize housing development, and improve housing accessibility for millions of Americans. The evidence from cities like Austin demonstrates that robust housing supply growth can accommodate population expansion while maintaining or improving affordability.
Congressional champions of this initiative will deliver tangible benefits to their constituents while addressing one of the nation’s most critical domestic challenges.

Global Reach: Netflix’s International Footprint

Question 1: How many countries does Netflix operate in?


Show Code
num_countries <- COUNTRY_TOP_10 |>
  summarise(total = n_distinct(country_name)) |>
  pull(total)








NoteKey Finding



Netflix operates in 94 countries worldwide, establishing itself as the world’s leading streaming entertainment service. This global reach enables Netflix to serve diverse audiences with both internationally appealing content and region-specific programming.
What this means: Netflix can distribute content globally while also tailoring offerings to regional preferences. This massive geographic footprint allows shows and movies to reach audiences they never could through traditional distribution.
Business Impact: More markets = more subscribers = larger budgets for original content


Top 20 Markets by Activity:


Show Code
COUNTRY_TOP_10 |>
  group_by(Country = country_name) |>
  summarise(
    `Total Top 10 Entries` = n(),
    `Unique Titles` = n_distinct(show_title),
    `Weeks of Data` = n_distinct(week),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(`Total Top 10 Entries`)) |>
  slice(1:20) |>
  datatable(
    caption = "Netflix's Most Active Markets",
    options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE)

plot_geo(netflix_countries) |>

text:
Content Length Analysis

Question 3: What is the longest film to appear in Netflix’s global Top 10?


Show Code
longest_film <- GLOBAL_TOP_10 |>
  filter(!is.na(runtime), grepl("Film", category)) |>
  arrange(desc(runtime)) |>
  slice(1)

longest_name <- longest_film$show_title
longest_minutes <- round(longest_film$runtime * 60)
longest_category <- longest_film$category








NoteKey Finding



Pushpa 2: The Rule (Reloaded Version) (Films (Non-English)) is the longest film in the Top 10 with a runtime of 224 minutes (3 hours, 44 minutes).
What makes this notable: This is a Telugu-language action film from India’s “Tollywood” cinema industry. At nearly 4 hours long, it’s longer than most Hollywood epics like Titanic (3h 14m) or The Lord of the Rings films.
The “Reloaded Version”: This extended cut is 24 minutes longer than the original theatrical release, showing how Netflix can offer director’s cuts and extended versions that wouldn’t work in traditional theaters.
Viewing Context: This runtime represents a serious time commitment—viewers spent almost 4 hours watching a single film, demonstrating intense audience engagement.
Note: Runtime data wasn’t tracked for older programs (pre-2022), so some classics may have been longer.


Runtime Comparison: Top 10 Longest Films


Show Code
GLOBAL_TOP_10 |>
  filter(!is.na(runtime), grepl("Film", category)) |>
  mutate(`Runtime (Minutes)` = round(runtime * 60)) |>
  group_by(`Film Title` = show_title, Category = category) |>
  summarise(
    `Runtime (Minutes)` = first(`Runtime (Minutes)`),
    `Weeks in Top 10` = max(cumulative_weeks_in_top_10),
    `Peak Rank` = min(weekly_rank),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(`Runtime (Minutes)`)) |>
  slice(1:10) |>
  mutate(Rank = row_number()) |>
  select(Rank, everything()) |>
  datatable(
    caption = "Longest Films in Netflix Global Top 10",
    options = list(pageLength = 10, dom = 't')
  )






Visual: How Long is “Too Long”?


Show Code
runtime_data <- GLOBAL_TOP_10 |>
  filter(!is.na(runtime), grepl("Film", category)) |>
  mutate(runtime_min = round(runtime * 60))

ggplot(runtime_data, aes(x = runtime_min)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#E50914", alpha = 0.7, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 90, linetype = "dashed", color = "blue", size = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 120, linetype = "dashed", color = "green", size = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = longest_minutes, linetype = "solid", color = "black", size = 1.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 90, y = 80, label = "Typical\n(90 min)", hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = 120, y = 70, label = "Long\n(2 hours)", hjust = -0.1, size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = longest_minutes, y = 60, 
           label = paste("Longest:", longest_minutes, "min"), 
           hjust = 1.1, size = 3, fontface = "bold") +
  labs(
    title = "Film Runtime Distribution on Netflix",
    subtitle = "Most films cluster around 90-120 minutes",
    x = "Runtime (minutes)",
    y = "Number of Films"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))










Industry Context:

Standard Feature: 90-120 minutes
Epic Length: 150+ minutes (2.5+ hours)
This Film: 224 minutes—2.5x longer than average

Despite its extreme length, this film spent 2 weeks in the Top 10, proving audiences will commit to longer runtimes for compelling content.

text:
Question 8: Red Notice Analysis

How many views did Red Notice receive in 2021?


Show Code
red_notice_runtime <- 1.97

red_notice_2021 <- GLOBAL_TOP_10 |>
  filter(show_title == "Red Notice", year(week) == 2021) |>
  summarise(
    total_hours = sum(weekly_hours_viewed, na.rm = TRUE),
    weeks = n()
  )

rn_hours <- red_notice_2021$total_hours
rn_views <- round(rn_hours / red_notice_runtime)
rn_million <- round(rn_views / 1e6, 1)








NoteKey Finding



Red Notice received approximately 201,390,863 views (201.4 million views) in 2021.
Calculation Method: - Total hours viewed: 396,740,000 - Runtime: 1 hour 58 minutes (1.97 hours) - Formula: Total Hours ÷ Runtime = Views - Result: 396,740,000 ÷ 1.97 = 201,390,863
Why This Matters: This was the most-watched film on Netflix until it was surpassed. The star-studded cast (Dwayne Johnson, Ryan Reynolds, Gal Gadot) and $200 million budget made it Netflix’s most expensive film at the time.

Regional Content Investment Yields Strong Engagement in World’s Most Populous Nation
Mumbai, India - October 2025
Netflix’s strategic investment in Hindi-language and regional Indian content continues to drive strong market performance, with 1168 unique titles charting in India’s Top 10 and demonstrating the effectiveness of localized programming.

“India represents one of our most important growth markets,” said Netflix’s Vice President of Content for India. “Our strategy of combining global hits with locally-produced content has resonated strongly with Indian audiences who want both international entertainment and stories that reflect their own experiences.”
Data reveals that several India-exclusive titles—programs that chart in India but not in Western markets—have achieved significant longevity. This validates Netflix’s approach of empowering local creators to tell authentic Indian stories rather than simply exporting Western content.
The company has announced plans to expand its Indian content slate in 2026, with new original series across multiple Indian languages and increased investment in regional film production.

NETFLIX’S INTERNATIONAL CONTENT BREAKS BARRIERS
Non-English Programming Achieves Unprecedented Global Success
Los Angeles, CA - October 2025
Netflix’s investment in international content continues to reshape global entertainment, with non-English programming now representing a major driver of platform engagement worldwide.
Global Content Milestones: - Non-English titles regularly chart in 90+ countries simultaneously - Record-breaking viewership from Korean, Spanish, and Indian productions - Increased investment in local-language originals across all regions - Growing audience acceptance of subtitled and dubbed content
“Our data proves that great storytelling transcends language barriers,” said Netflix’s Head of Global TV. “When we invest in authentic, high-quality content from creators worldwide, audiences everywhere respond enthusiastically.”
Recent successes like Squid Game (Korean), Money Heist (Spanish), and All Quiet on the Western Front (German) have shattered previous records, with some non-English titles outperforming major English-language releases. This trend validates Netflix’s continued commitment to diverse, global storytelling.
The company reports that subtitle and dub viewership has grown substantially year-over-year, with viewers increasingly comfortable consuming content from different cultures. This shift represents a fundamental change in how global audiences discover and enjoy entertainment.
Netflix plans to further expand its international production capabilities in 2026, with new production hubs in Southeast Asia, Africa, and Eastern Europe.
About Netflix: Netflix is the world’s leading streaming entertainment service with over 260 million paid memberships in over 190 countries.

title: Netflix Global Streaming Analysis
text:
Strategic Insights from the Data
This comprehensive analysis of Netflix’s Top 10 data reveals a streaming service executing successfully across multiple strategic dimensions:

Key Takeaways:

Global Scale: Operating in 94 countries enables Netflix to amortize content costs across a massive subscriber base, making big-budget productions economically viable.
The Localization Paradox: Netflix succeeds by being both global and local—distributing worldwide while investing in region-specific content that resonates with local audiences (India example).
The Long Tail Wins: Shows like Stranger Things that maintain Top 10 status for years generate more total value than flashy debuts that fade quickly.
Language Barriers Are Falling: Non-English content regularly achieves global success, validating Netflix’s investment in international productions.
Data-Driven Decision Making: Netflix’s Top 10 transparency allows both internal teams and external analysts to identify what works, informing future content investments.



The “Gourmet Cheeseburger” Philosophy Validated
Netflix’s goal of creating “gourmet cheeseburgers”—high-quality content with mass appeal—is clearly working:

Stranger Things: Critical acclaim + 2,595,530,000 hours viewed
Squid Game: Cultural phenomenon + 5.05 billion hours viewed

All Quiet on the Western Front: 4 Oscars + 23 weeks in Top 10

These aren’t trade-offs between quality and popularity—they achieve both simultaneously.


Looking Forward
As streaming competition intensifies, Netflix’s early investments in: - International production infrastructure - Multi-language dubbing and subtitling - Data analytics and recommendation systems - Creator relationships worldwide
…provide sustainable competitive advantages that newer entrants will struggle to replicate.
The data shows Netflix isn’t just surviving the streaming wars—it’s defining how global entertainment works in the 21st century.

title: Netflix Global Streaming Analysis
text:
Technical Notes

Data Sources

Global Top 10: Netflix’s weekly global rankings with viewership hours
Country Top 10: Country-specific weekly rankings (rankings only, no hours)
Time Period: 2020-present (October 2025)
Update Frequency: Weekly



Data Limitations

Historical Coverage: Top 10 tracking began in 2020, so earlier content (like Stranger Things Season 1) isn’t captured
Runtime Availability: Runtime data wasn’t tracked for older entries (pre-2022)
Country-Level Details: Country dataset doesn’t include viewership hours, only rankings
Viewing Calculation: Views calculated by dividing total hours by runtime (approximation)



Methodology

Views Formula: Total Hours Viewed ÷ Runtime = Approximate Views
Weeks Counting: Used n_distinct(week) to count unique weeks, handling non-consecutive appearances
Filtering: Excluded reality/competition spin-offs (e.g., “Squid Game: The Challenge”) from scripted series analysis



Analysis Completed: November 03, 2025
Data Source: Netflix Top 10 Portal
Analyst: Swarnadeep Roy

This analysis was prepared for Netflix’s Public Relations team to support press releases highlighting successful content and strategic market performance.
